summary: This standards-track document defines the Network Configuration Access Control Model (NACM) for NETCONF and RESTCONF. It provides a standard way to control which users may read, change or run operations on configuration data. The goal is secure, multi-vendor interoperable management that people can use easily.

plainLanguage.summary: NACM is the standard permission system for NETCONF and RESTCONF, the two protocols used to manage network devices. It lets an administrator decide which users may read, change, or run which commands. Before NACM, neither protocol had a shared rule for this, so each deployment had to invent its own.

what are the nacm crudx access rights
how does restconf map to nacm
subtitle: The standard permission system for NETCONF and RESTCONF: who may read, change or run what on a managed device.

tldr.problem: NETCONF and RESTCONF provide no standard way to restrict which protocol operations and which content each user may access, so controlled, interoperable access was not possible.
tldr.mechanism: NACM groups users and applies ordered permit or deny rules per group over modules, protocol operations, data nodes and notifications using five rights (create, read, update, delete, execute), falling back to global defaults when no rule matches.
tldr.outcome: It is an Internet Standard that obsoletes RFC 6536, adds RESTCONF support and covers the YANG 1.1 action and notification statements; no later RFC obsoletes or updates it.

today: RFC 8341 is an Internet Standard (STD 91) and obsoletes RFC 6536; the unit metadata lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What NACM Is For
sections.content:
The Network Configuration Protocol (NETCONF, RFC 6241) and the RESTCONF protocol (RFC 8040) do not provide any standard mechanism to restrict the protocol operations and content that each user is authorized to access. RFC 8341 defines the NETCONF Access Control Model (NACM) for the Operations and Content layers of both protocols. It has three main parts: access control design objectives, the model itself, and a YANG data model (ietf-netconf-acm.yang).

The RFC obsoletes RFC 6536. The changes since that document add support for two constructs new in YANG 1.1 (RFC 7950): the action statement, which works like rpc but sits inside a data node, and the notification statement inside a data node. Because these live inside the data tree, access to one specific instance can be controlled, which top-level rpc and notification statements cannot do.

The update also adds RESTCONF support, clarifies that a data node path match includes descendant nodes, and states that write access is not required for data nodes modified only as a side effect, such as when a YANG when expression changes its result.
sections.plainLanguage: Network devices can be changed remotely, but neither management protocol said who was allowed to do what. NACM is the shared rulebook for both. This version replaces an older RFC and adds rules for newer YANG features and for RESTCONF.

sections.title: Design Objectives
sections.content:
Server vendors can add custom protocol operations, so a model cannot simply list the standard ones. NACM therefore protects three conceptual control points: protocol operation (may this operation be invoked), datastore (may these data nodes be read or altered) and notification (may this event type be received).

The other objectives shape how the model is used. It should be simple: one rule set for operations, data and notifications, with a small, familiar set of permissions. Rules must work for a single user or configurable groups, and the mapping from users to groups may be delegated to a central server such as a RADIUS server (RFC 2865). Enforcement must be possible to disable without deleting any rules, and configuration must go through a standard YANG data model.

The RFC also asks that security-sensitive content be identified in machine-readable form. Relying on documentation alone forces administrators to study each new data model, and it leaves a window of vulnerability after the model is loaded but before the matching rules are configured. A model designer should be able to tag content that must be protected by default, so tools can deny access to it automatically.
sections.plainLanguage: The rules have to guard three doors: running commands, reading or changing settings, and receiving alerts. The model also had to stay simple, because a permission system nobody understands will not be used.

sections.title: Where the Checks Happen
sections.content:
NACM provides independent control of RPC, action, data and notification access. It supports an emergency recovery session that bypasses all access control, so a broken configuration can be repaired. It uses one small set of datastore permissions, supports YANG security tags such as nacm:default-deny-write, provides separate defaults for read, write and execute, applies rules to groups of users, can be switched off at runtime for debugging, and exposes counters of denied requests that a client can monitor.

For each active session, access control is applied to every <rpc> message except <close-session>, unless the session is a recovery session. The server first checks whether the user may invoke the protocol operation, then checks each data node the operation touches. For an action, read access is required for every data node in the hierarchy that identifies the action, and execute access for the action node itself. For example, to use /interfaces/interface/reset-interface a group must be able to read /interfaces and /interfaces/interface and execute the action.

For notifications, read access is required for the notification event type and, when the notification sits inside a data subtree, for the nodes that identify it. A notification the user may not read is dropped for that subscription. RESTCONF operations are mapped onto the same model based on the HTTP method and resource class: a POST on a data resource counts as write access, while a POST on an operation resource counts as execute access.
sections.plainLanguage: Every request passes two guards. One asks whether the user may run the command at all; the other checks each piece of data the command needs. Alerts get their own check before the server delivers them.

sections.title: Datastore Access and RESTCONF
sections.content:
The same access control rules apply to every datastore that supports NACM, and all conventional configuration datastores plus the operational state datastore are covered. Local files, remote files and datastores reached through the <url> parameter are not. Access is expressed with five hard-wired rights, abbreviated CRUDX: create, read, update, delete and execute. New datastores can be mapped onto these rights if they have similar access semantics.

RESTCONF methods are translated to NETCONF operations for access control. HEAD and GET are reads; POST on a datastore or data resource is create, while POST on an operation resource is execute; PUT on data is create and update, and on a datastore it is copy-config with update; PATCH is update and DELETE is delete. OPTIONS is not subject to NACM at all.

Some NETCONF operations get special treatment. For <get> and <get-config>, nodes the client may not read are silently omitted along with their descendants, so filters keep working instead of failing with an error. An <edit-config> that would create, delete or modify a node without the matching right is rejected with access-denied, but nodes changed only as implicit side effects need no rights. <delete-config> and <kill-session> are denied by default and the exec default does not apply to them; <discard-changes> needs only execute permission on the operation.
sections.plainLanguage: Everyone gets up to five kinds of key: make something new, look, change, remove, or run. Web-style requests are translated into those same keys, and a denied read simply leaves the data out of the answer.

sections.title: Users, Groups, Switches and Rules
sections.content:
A user is a name derived from the transport layer when the session is established; if the transport layer cannot authenticate the user, the session is terminated. Access is granted to groups, not to users: a group has a unique name and zero or more member usernames, and one user can belong to several groups. A server MAY support an emergency recovery session that bypasses all access control, which is useful for repairing a broken configuration; how such a session is identified is implementation specific.

Five global controls shape enforcement. enable-nacm turns the whole system on or off: when it is false, every request is permitted. read-default, write-default and exec-default choose permit or deny when no rule matches. enable-external-groups decides whether group names reported by the transport layer are used.

There are four kinds of rule. A module rule covers definitions in one YANG module. A protocol operation rule covers one operation, named by its module and operation name. A data node rule covers a data node and its descendants, named by path. A notification rule covers one notification event type. Rules sit inside ordered rule lists that apply to named groups.
sections.plainLanguage: Rules are written for teams, not for individuals. A master switch turns the whole system off, four default answers decide what happens when no rule fits, and a spare key is kept for emergencies.

sections.title: How a Request Is Decided
sections.content:
The server MUST use the rules in effect when it starts processing a message, and those same rules MUST stay in effect for the whole message. Access control is not applied to server-initiated access such as loading the running configuration at boot. If no access control configuration exists at first startup, the server MUST NOT allow any write access to a session role except a recovery session.

A protocol operation is authorized in a fixed order. The request is permitted at once if enable-nacm is false, if the session is a recovery session, or if the operation is <close-session>. Otherwise the server collects the user's groups, adding external groups when they are enabled, walks the rule lists in configuration order, and applies the first rule that matches. If nothing matches, an operation tagged nacm:default-deny-all is denied, <kill-session> and <delete-config> are denied, and otherwise exec-default decides.

Data node access follows the same pattern: a path rule matches the node it names and its descendants, and the fallbacks are nacm:default-deny-write, nacm:default-deny-all, then the read, write and execute defaults. The server MUST NOT reveal information the client may not read in <error-info> or in restricted node contents in an <rpc-error>; a denied read simply omits the data from the reply. Notifications the user may not read are dropped for that subscription.
sections.plainLanguage: The server checks the master switch, then reads the rule list from top to bottom and obeys the first rule that fits. If none fits, it uses the configured default. A refusal never leaks the data it was hiding.

sections.title: The ietf-netconf-acm YANG Module
sections.content:
NACM is configured through a YANG module whose top container is /nacm. It holds the five global switches, three read-only counters (denied-operations, denied-data-writes and denied-notifications), a groups list, and an ordered rule-list list. Each rule carries a name, a module-name, an optional rule type (protocol operation, notification, or data node path), an access-operations mask, an action of permit or deny, and an optional comment.

The module is the normative content that a server MUST support. Because the rule lists are ordered by the client, the server evaluates them in the order they appear in the running configuration datastore. The IANA section updates the registration of ietf-netconf-acm (prefix nacm) in the YANG Module Names registry to reference RFC 8341 instead of RFC 6536.
sections.plainLanguage: The whole rulebook lives in one standard YANG module, so any device and any management tool can read and edit it the same way.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The mandatory-to-implement secure transport for NETCONF is SSH (RFC 6242) and for RESTCONF is TLS. The RFC warns that responses to RESTCONF OPTIONS and PATCH must not vary with whether a resource exists, because that could be used to probe for values; servers should return access-denied before exposing any instance information.

Administrators are told to check the defaults: enable-nacm is true, read-default is permit, write-default is deny and exec-default is permit. They should restrict write and read access to the NACM data itself, make sure the mapping from transport identity to username is unique and correct, and set enable-external-groups to false when the protocol that supplies group names, such as RADIUS, does not resist man-in-the-middle attacks.

Other risks include repeated edit attempts that reveal whether hidden data exists ("fishing"), non-standard operations with undocumented side effects, data that aliases sensitive data, leafref values that expose other nodes, and datastore locking used for denial of service, which is why the RFC suggests restricting exec access to <lock>, <unlock>, <partial-lock> and <partial-unlock>. Data model designers should mark sensitive nodes with nacm:default-deny-write or nacm:default-deny-all.
sections.plainLanguage: A rulebook works only when it is set up well. Check the default answers, protect the rulebook itself, and do not let repeated guesses reveal what is hidden.

viz.caption: THE FOUR RULE TYPES IN NACM

items.title: Module rule
items.text: Controls access for definitions in a specific YANG module, identified by name.

items.title: Protocol operation rule
items.text: Controls one protocol operation, identified by its YANG module and name.

items.title: Data node rule
items.text: Controls a data node and its descendants, identified by path.

items.title: Notification rule
items.text: Controls one notification event type, identified by its YANG module and name.
